qasa7:204: The author designs a subtle thought experiment: suppose a learner acquires a language only by predicting the next word, with no semantic knowledge whatsoever. In that case, we cannot tell whether we are asking for a summary, elaboration, or paraphrase, because we do not understand the language—likewise, translation cannot be verified. This reveals why, when we interact with LLMs in a language we know well, we unconsciously project our own semantic framework onto model outputs: we attribute structure and coherence to the model because we interpret its outputs from within our shared semantic framework. That attribution is misleading and does not constitute evidence that the model has genuine internal semantics.

wiv8fv:293: "A scalpel is a surgical instrument" (analytic truth, true in virtue of meaning itself) and "A scalpel is sharp" (synthetic truth, true in virtue of worldly facts) are both reproduced correctly on the surface by an LLM, but the LLM cannot distinguish them. The reason: the LLM has no mechanism for judging whether a statement is "meaning-constituted" or "world-dependent," let alone for recognizing which statements fall into which category. "A scalpel is a surgical instrument" appears in training data not as a rule or definition, but merely as a token sequence with particular statistical features. This directly rules out the propositional attitude of "knowing that something is true" for LLMs.
